I have a directory (.github) for Github Copilot. I am working on creating a process with agents / subagents that can reliably work through work QUICKLY in parallel with minimal Human-In-The-Loop interactions for inane low-value tasks (e.g. 'approve this command to run').

I have experimented with 'beads', the 'memory tool' (which really is a local issue tracker that allows for efficient context window usage). This is incredibly useful for keeping track of (in multiple git branches or worktrees) what is currently in-flight.

What I am ideating on is a multi-step process (I have an 'alpha' version in the shared code) which allows for:

1. **planning** - creating a high-level plan that (should) include the context, problem to be solved (purpose), goals, acceptance criteria, and approach. This process would include the user providing a 'seed' of an idea and then iterating until it matches what is expected. In enterprises, this should 'feed back' into a GitHub issue or Jira ticket to make the work stream visible (ideally it would _start_ from there, and it *could* but in many cases the PRD is incomplete or not suitable for decomposition as what an Agentic workflow would require). To keep things simple we can start with the assumption that all work is controlled _within_ this process, and in the future we could expand to accommodate work done _outside_ this process as it is fed into the process. I would like github issues to be used to keep track of the 'who, what, when, where, why' (if not the how) - but for simplicity, we can start with 'beads' as the source of truth and later expand to including external systems as 'shadow' tracking systems that _reflect_ what 'beads' produces. I am imagining the output of the 'planning' process could be an ephemeral markdown file that is ultimately removed - as these 'plans' do not represent living documents and often get out-of-sync, where as a series of issues that are tracked (e.g. 'beads') offers a history of changes that are more reliably understood (and the 'current open problems' become much clearer and navigable by the command line, to reduce swamping the context window on large projects that span many years).

2. **decomposition** - after the human approves the plan my hope is that an order-of-operations and dependencies could be discovered in a 'decomposition' process. At this stage, an 'internal' representation of what needs to happen (perhaps even formalised into a Directed Acyclical Graph of work-to-be-done) in what order (preferably with parallelisation called out, as if many software engineers were available to work on the tasks). The idea is that each 'deliverable' could happen independently of one another, with limited scope. Each 'deliverable' would include it's own 'context, problem to be solved, goals, accceptance criteria, and approach' - a mini version of the larger plan; the results could be as little as a single line of code changed (although more realistically the work would be broken up into somewhat larger chunks depending on what kind of work 'hangs together' well). Ideally at this stage the output would be 'beads' issues created with meaningful titles and descriptions (descriptions are where the 'context, problem to be solved, goals, acceptance criteria, and approach' would live) _and_ dependencies would be represented there. The hope would be the DAG would minimize the amount of 'clock time' of the work to be done, as well as minimize the merge conflicts to be resolved.

Output: 'beads' issues that reflect the Directed Acyclical Graph of work to be done.

3. **spawn** - this one is tricky. This would require some sort of 'long running process' that spawns a 'wave' of tasks into subagents (either locally in git worktrees or in the cloud in git branches) and then 'watches' (polls) for whether they have finished or not, and I imagine in practice it would need to 'intelligently' (e.g. non-deterministically, using a foundation model) resolve merge conflicts (whether in the cloud or locally).

There is also the consideration of _which_ agent to spawn - for example, one could spawn a 'copilot' agent (generic) but there may be instances where guidance for testing (if it is a testing task) or refactoring (if a refactoring task) could be used. I have imagined that if using Claude Code, 'hooks' or 'skills' or 'agents' or 'mcp servers' could help here - especially the deterministic 'hooks' for running a long-running job that just checks to see if the subagents have finished or timed out. I wouldn't know how to reliably or robustly do this with Github Copilot but I'm open to ideas.

4. **sync** - [optional?] this could control the 'spawning' of a new wave once a wave has completed - perhaps the agents ping-pong back and forth between 'spawning' and 'syncing' until all the relevant tickets have been completed. One word of warning of course is that the 'beads' may contain irrelevant issues that were created at some other point and put in the backlog and have not been completed. I imagine those would ideally be ignored.

## Benefits of this Approach

I have played with AI Agents and have seen how powerful they can be - some models like Claude Opus 4.5 (newly released) is *incredibly powerful* at planning. Others, like Claude Haiku 4.5 and Raptor Mini (newly released by Github Copilot) are extremely useful for more targeted 'execution' of work (even though their context windows are quite broad and can bring in a lot of context before executing!).

Software engineering is an iterative process that generally follows a pattern: planning, decomposition, execution is roughly that pattern. Of course, there are a _ton_ of nuance on what is being planned and how it is executed. Ideally within the execution loop, general rules and approaches are followed - such as unit and integration testing, running linting tools (can happen deterministically as part of pre-commit hooks, but sometimes linting tools have errors or warnings that appear that require 'manual' intervention, e.g. Agentic intervention). As much as this process is predictable, it is automatable.

A control 'loop' and non-deterministic models that can recover from errors offers an opportunity to put guardrails and checks on progress (stages for 'human-in-the-loop' interactions) while 'boosting' the more tedious and repetitive aspects of software engineering. Planning naturally becomes more weighted in terms of how much effort is put in, while execution becomes nearly trivial. Or at least, that's the goal.

By breaking up the stages into smaller chunks, work gets done faster and is more targeted.
